User: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $88,100. Side income: $14,600 from web design (2 clients). Interest $1,780 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Robinhood). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (EdFinancial, 2017–2020); charity $1,100 to Local United Way with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
Assistant: I can help — below I’ll (1) walk through how your income and deductions look, (2) compare standard vs. itemized, (3) explain home-office treatment (actual vs simplified), (4) list the tax forms you’ll use, and (5) flag a few questions/next steps so the numbers are accurate.

Summary of amounts you gave
- Filing status: Married filing jointly (Seattle, WA — no state income tax)
- W-2 (Acme): $88,100
- Side/self-employment (web design, 2 clients): $14,600
- Interest (Chase savings): $1,780
- Dividends (Robinhood): $440
- Rent: $1,600/month → $19,200/year; apartment = 680 sq ft; home office = 155 sq ft
- Student loan interest paid: $4,400 (2017–2020 loans)
- Charitable donations (cash, with receipt): $1,100
- “Unreimbursed expenses”: $720

Key clarifying questions before finalizing numbers
- Does your spouse have any wage/investment/self-employment income you need included (you said MFJ but only gave your amounts)?
- Are the $720 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses related to your web design (supplies, software, travel, etc.), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses? (If they’re business expenses for your self-employment, they’re deductible on Schedule C; if they’re unreimbursed employee expenses, they’re not deductible on the federal return.)
- Does your rent include utilities? (For actual home-office allocation this matters; if utilities are separate, you’d allocate them too.)
- Is the 155 sq ft used exclusively and regularly for the web-design business (required for home-office deduction)?

Preliminary calculations and treatment (estimates)
1) Gross income
- W-2: 88,100
- Self-employment (gross): 14,600
- Interest: 1,780
- Dividends: 440
Total gross income = 104,920

2) Home-office allocation
- Office % = 155 / 680 = 0.2279 ≈ 22.8%

If you use the actual-expense method:
- Rent portion allocated to business = 22.8% × $19,200 = ≈ $4,377 (this is a Schedule C business expense)

If you use the simplified method:
- Deduction = $5 × 155 sq ft = $775 (no Form 8829 needed)

Actual method yields a much larger home-office deduction here (≈$4,377 vs $775) assuming rent (and possibly utilities, renter’s ins.) can be allocated.

3) Business expenses and net self-employment income
Assuming the $720 are legitimate business expenses:
- Business expenses total = $4,377 (home-office rent share) + $720 = $5,097
- Net self-employment profit = 14,600 − 5,097 = $9,503

If the $720 are not business expenses, net SE income = 14,600 − 4,377 = $10,223 (use whichever is accurate).

4) Self-employment tax (estimate) and adjustment
- SE tax is computed on 92.35% of net SE earnings and is ~15.3% of that amount.
Using net = $9,503: taxable SE earnings ≈ 0.9235×9,503 ≈ 8,776 → SE tax ≈ 8,776×0.153 ≈ $1,343.
Half of that SE tax (~$672) is an above-the-line deduction (reported on Schedule 1), which reduces AGI.

5) Student loan interest deduction
- Maximum allowable deduction = $2,500 (subject to income phaseouts). You reported paying $4,400, so the maximum you can claim (if you’re eligible based on MAGI limits) is $2,500.
- For married filing jointly the deduction phases out at higher incomes — based on the AGI we estimate below you are likely under the phaseout threshold, but I’ll confirm after you answer about spouse income.

6) Schedules/required reporting for interest/dividends
- Because your interest is $1,780 (> $1,500), you must file Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) with Form 1040.
- Dividends ($440) are also reported on Schedule B/1040.

7) Rough AGI / taxable income estimate (using assumptions above)
Start: Total income = $104,920
Less:
- half SE tax ≈ $672 (adjustment)
- student loan interest deduction (if fully allowed) = $2,500
Adjusted gross income (approx) ≈ 104,920 − 672 − 2,500 = 101,748

Standard deduction (2024, married filing jointly) = $29,200 (IRS inflation-adjusted amount for 2024)
Estimated taxable income ≈ 101,748 − 29,200 = 72,548 (this is a ballpark — final will vary with exact SE tax and spouse income)

8) Standard vs itemized comparison
- Itemized items you listed: charity $1,100
- You didn’t list mortgage interest, significant property taxes, state income tax (WA has none), medical expenses, or other large itemized items.
- Given the standard deduction (~$29,200) compared to the itemized total you provided (~$1,100), you should take the standard deduction — it will give a larger reduction of taxable income.
Note: the home-office deduction does NOT depend on itemizing — it’s claimed on Schedule C (self-employment), so you still get that benefit whether you itemize or take the standard deduction.

9) Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (possible additional reduction)
- As a self-employed sole proprietor, you may be eligible for a QBI deduction up to 20% of qualified business income (rough estimate: 20% × your net SE profit, e.g., ≈ $1,900). There are income thresholds and other limits, but given your taxable income estimate, you’ll likely be eligible for the simplified 20% QBI (Form 8995). This can further reduce taxable income. I can run a more exact number if you confirm spouse income and final net SE profit.

Which IRS forms you’ll use (primary)
- Form 1040 — main individual tax form
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — adjustments to income (where student loan interest and half SE-tax deduction appear)
- Schedule B (Form 1040) — interest and ordinary dividends (because interest > $1,500)
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — Profit or Loss from Business (report your web-design gross receipts and business expenses, including home-office allocation if using actual)
- Schedule SE — Self-Employment Tax (compute SE tax and the deductible half)
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (use this if you take the actual-expense method for the home-office deduction) — this supports the actual allocation and ties to Schedule C
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — Qualified Business Income Deduction (if you claim QBI)
- Keep supporting documents but you don’t file them (receipts for charity, student loan interest statement Form 1098-E, rent/utility records, records of business expenses, etc.)

Recommendations / next steps
1. Confirm the clarifying items I asked above (spouse income; whether $720 are business expenses; whether rent includes utilities; whether office is exclusive and regular).
2. If the $720 are business expenses, include them on Schedule C. If they are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are not deductible.
3. Use the actual home-office method (with Form 8829) if your rent/utilities allocation is accurate and the workspace meets the exclusive-and-regular-use test — it will likely produce a larger deduction than the simplified $5/sq ft method in your case.
4. Claim the student loan interest deduction on Schedule 1 up to $2,500 if your MAGI is below the phaseout for MFJ — confirm spouse income to be sure you’re not in a phaseout.
5. File Schedule B because interest > $1,500.
6. Pay attention to SE tax and estimated taxes — if you haven’t been having taxes withheld or making estimated payments on the self-employment income, you may owe SE tax and additional income tax (and possible estimated-payment penalties). Consider estimated payments for next year if self-employment continues.
7. Consider QBI (Form 8995) — I can calculate it for you once you confirm net SE profit and spouse income.

If you want, I can:
- Recalculate the numbers precisely if you tell me spouse income and confirm whether the $720 are business expenses and whether rent includes utilities.
- Prepare a checklist of documents and receipts to gather before you file.
- Draft a summary you can hand to your tax preparer with the numbers and forms to use.

Which of those would you like next?
